item.title: Republicans Caught in a Bind With Trump as Midterms Near
item.description:
President Trump has been the most potent force in Republican primary elections, elevating allies and foiling foes with endorsements, social media posts and rally appearances.

But as the end of primary season draws near and the sprint to the general election begins, Mr. Trump may soon be something entirely different for Republican candidates. A liability.

The president’s approval rating is well underwater, dragged down by rising prices and an unpopular war. And Democrats have made clear that they hope to target Republican candidates in battleground races by tying them to Mr. Trump, believing they can ride voter anger with his administration to congressional majorities.

Yet Republicans in competitive contests may still need him. Even as they look for ways to distance themselves from Mr. Trump to appeal to swing voters, they must also weigh the president’s hold on their party’s base and his tendency to lash out at Republican dissenters.

“It’s a difficult one,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist in Texas, adding that the president’s approach to the primaries had probably made the dilemma harder for candidates, but predicting they would increasingly seek separation from him. “I think it’ll be very subtle. I think it’ll be district by district.”

Many Republicans are hoping for financial support from the president’s well-funded but tightfisted super PAC, MAGA Inc., which came to the rescue of Senator Darline Graham in her hotly contested Republican runoff this week. The group flooded the contest with more than $800,000 worth of voter calls and text messages.

There are signs of deeper involvement to come in races against Democrats. At a meeting in the Oval Office this month, Mr. Trump met with senior advisers and a small number of ad makers who had signed up with MAGA Inc., according to two people briefed on the meeting, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private conversation. The existence of the meeting was first reported by The Atlantic.

The gathering included a discussion about Democrats’ plans to make the election a referendum on Mr. Trump, and the president made clear that he wanted the advertising to include a robust defense of his record, according to the people briefed on the meeting. It was unclear how big of a share commercials focused on Mr. Trump would take of a fall ad campaign.

Spending by the group could be a welcome development for Republicans. As political headwinds have strengthened against them in the spring and summer, they have been holding out hope that MAGA Inc. would begin to invest in a challenging midterm cycle. But a rush of spending could also offer another way for the president to tighten his grip on the party — and on candidates who are angling for a measure of independence.

Mr. Trump, who has managed to revive his standing after past spells of widespread unpopularity, has started to put himself at the center of the midterms. He has urged supporters to “pretend” he is on the ballot and suggested he will spend significant campaign cash reserves.

Democrats are just as eager for him to play a starring role. Representative Jamie Raskin, Democrat of Maryland, argued that congressional Republicans had been boxed in by the president and rendered little more than a rubber stamp for his agenda.

“Donald Trump controls the Republican caucus in Congress like a bunch of trained seals,” Mr. Raskin said Wednesday as he headed to a campaign event for Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate for Senate in Michigan. “This is essentially what the November elections are about.”

One of the biggest variables on the minds of Republicans is money. The president has kept them guessing about how MAGA Inc. might deploy its massive war chest.

Mr. Trump continues to fund-raise, but he has been far less willing to part with the record sums he has accumulated.

“I’ll be spending a lot of that money and my own money,” Mr. Trump told reporters last week, though he has not spent any of his personal funds on politics in a decade. “But I’ll be spending a lot of that money for candidates that I think are good.”

At a briefing for Republican senators in early August by two of Mr. Trump’s advisers and the leader of the Senate Republican super PAC, the Trump team left the strong impression that money was coming imminently as they offered messaging advice, according to two people who attended the meeting and spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private discussion.

But in the weeks since, MAGA Inc. has not been spending in Senate battleground states, and some Republicans are growing anxious that races in North Carolina and Georgia may be falling out of reach.

“MAGA Inc. is sitting on a small nation’s G.D.P., and certainly their money is welcomed,” said Mike Hahn, a Republican strategist working for the party’s Senate nominee in Georgia, Representative Mike Collins. He said he would welcome Trump-focused ads in Mr. Collins’s race against Senator Jon Ossoff.

A number of battleground Republicans — including former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan, a Senate candidate; Representative Mike Lawler of New York; and Representative Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin — have joined the president at events since the spring. Others have said they would be open to it.

A spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, Mike Marinella, said House Republicans were eager to campaign with the president because of his ability to energize the party’s base.

Still, some Republicans have shown little visible interest. They include Senator Susan Collins of Maine and the Senate candidate Michele Tafoya of Minnesota. And in Iowa, Representative Ashley Hinson, a Trump ally running in a competitive Senate race, has pushed back on his decision to allow beef to be imported into the United States with lower tariffs.

The White House has said that the president is committed to maintaining Republican majorities and that its policies have given the party a compelling platform to run on. “There is a great story to tell,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement, pointing to steep decreases in crime and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

It is not yet clear how much pressure Mr. Trump might place on vulnerable Republicans to offer him total loyalty. Nor is it clear how interventions by Mr. Trump in favor of members of his party in competitive general-election races would play with voters.

Republicans have found reasons for disappointment in each of the last the two cycles when Mr. Trump himself was not on the ballot, losing the House in the 2018 midterm elections and failing to recover the Senate in the 2022. (They did win the House in 2022.)

Mr. Trump has pointed to those outcomes as he pushes voters to turn out in the midterms.

“They say that ‘Trump does great when he’s on the ballot, but when he’s not on the ballot, his people don’t come,’” the president said at a rally in South Carolina last week. He added, “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote.”

Days later, Mr. Trump showed he could draw enough Republicans to the polls to elevate Ms. Graham in the Senate primary runoff, even after she fumbled in a debate when she admitted to not being “that informed on national security.”

Mr. Trump’s actions during primary races could influence the November election.

The president spent the spring on a retribution tour, investing heavily in his successful efforts to oust Senators Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and John Cornyn of Texas, as well as Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky. Mr. Cassidy and Mr. Massie hail from deeply conservative areas, while Mr. Cornyn’s state is seen as increasingly competitive.

Mr. Trump’s effort to oust Mr. Cornyn, who had said in 2023 that Mr. Trump’s time had “passed him by,” helped hand the Republican Senate nomination to Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general. Many Republicans say that Mr. Paxton could offer Democrats an opportunity to win a Senate seat in Texas for the first time in decades.

The president has been more restrained in targeting other battleground Republicans. In March, he restored his primary endorsement of a Colorado Republican, Representative Jeff Hurd, after his short-lived support for a right-wing challenger generated backlash from Republicans who warned it would imperil the seat in November.

The episode underscored Mr. Trump’s competing impulses — a desire for party fealty and a fear of losing Congress in the midterms. Mr. Hurd had criticized the president’s tariff policies, plainly irritating him. But Mr. Trump still backed down.

And even if candidates like Ms. Collins, who is running for re-election in Democratic-leaning Maine, may be granted more space for dissent by the president, they may also find it hard to disentangle themselves from his falling standing.

“Like it or not, politics today is about President Trump,” said Allen Fuller, a Republican consultant in Colorado, adding: “In the past you could localize your campaign and run a good ground game, do a lot of in-district events and you’d be OK. You can’t do that in 2026.”

Democrats say that general-election voters across the country will punish Republicans who have tied themselves to the unpopular president.

“Republicans have been unwilling to stand up to Trump policies,” Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, the chair of the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm, said in an interview last week. “Voters are going to vote differently. If they voted for Trump the last time, I don’t know that they’ll vote for a Republican this time.”

Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting.

item.title: Democrats to Force Senate Vote on Israel’s Human Rights Practices
item.description:
Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, on Thursday plans to introduce a resolution that would order the Trump administration to provide Congress with a detailed accounting of Israel’s human rights practices in the West Bank, laying the groundwork to force a vote on the matter in coming weeks.

The measure, the latest bid by Democrats in Congress to challenge the policies and actions of Israel’s government, invokes a provision of the Foreign Assistance Act that allows lawmakers to request information from the State Department about the human rights record of any country receiving U.S. security assistance.

Co-signed by 10 Senate Democrats, the resolution is privileged, meaning that Mr. Van Hollen could force a vote on it even if Republican leaders refuse, as expected, to bring it to the floor. That could lead to yet another vote in Congress showcasing Democrats’ divide over Israel as a growing contingent in the party turns against the Jewish state.

“We’ve seen ongoing human rights violations on the West Bank, but we’re going from bad to abysmal,” Mr. Van Hollen said in an interview.

The resolution focuses on at least nine U.S. citizens who have been killed in the West Bank since January 2022, including Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian American journalist killed in 2022, and Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, who was fatally shot by an Israeli soldier in 2024. It argues that Israeli authorities have failed to punish those responsible and that American agencies have failed to conduct their own independent investigations or provide substantive information about existing ones.

“If the United States Senate shines a spotlight on this, we will save lives,” Mr. Van Hollen said. “We will save the lives of American citizens. We will also save the lives of Palestinian civilians.”

Concern about violence in the West Bank has steadily grown among Democrats in Congress. Last year, Senator Cory Booker, Democrat of New Jersey, introduced the West Bank Violence Prevention Act, which Mr. Van Hollen cosponsored, to impose visa and financial sanctions on people who commit or facilitate violence against civilians there. The bill attracted broad Democratic support but did not advance out of the Republican-led Foreign Relations Committee and was never brought up for a vote.

J Street, the liberal pro-Israel advocacy group that backed that legislation, has argued that sanctions are needed to disrupt networks supporting extremist settlers and Palestinian militant groups and preserve the possibility of a two-state solution. The group has cited estimates that settler violence rose 30 percent during the first months of 2025 compared with the same period a year earlier.

The issue has also prompted unusually sharp criticism from Israeli officials. Yechiel Leiter, Israel’s ambassador to the United States and a longtime settler, said earlier this year that extremist settler violence was a “stain” on Israel and was costing the country support in Washington. He said the Israeli government was taking this seriously.

The issue has gained renewed focus this month following a new spate of violence in the West Bank with extremists settlers trapping two Palestinian families in their homes in the Israeli-occupied territories. One of the homes is owned by Louai Abu Ridi, an American citizen, prompting condemnation from U.S. officials including Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, who called the actions of the settlers “thuggish” and said Israeli Defense Forces and local police had acted at his urging to “remove the Israeli terrorists doing this.”

“Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting,” Mr. Huckabee said in a social media post earlier this month.

Shortly after, Mr. Leiter echoed the remarks, saying in his own post that “you cannot settle the land through destabilizing and disruptive behavior, as my esteemed colleague Mike Huckabee brilliantly put it when he spoke of ‘unsettling behavior.’”

Extremist settlers have carried out at least 1,380 attacks in 250 communities in 2026, according to U.N. data from late July. Those settlers have faced a near-total lack of consequences.

Mr. Van Hollen’s resolution would draw in the legislative branch to confront the issue directly.

It would give the secretary of state 30 days to provide congressional committees with an unclassified report detailing what American officials know about the killings, the status of investigations and the identities of potential suspects and Israeli security units involved.

The administration would also have to determine whether credible information implicates any Israeli security units in such violence.

The resolution also demands information about Palestinian children held under Israeli military law, including allegations of torture and other mistreatment.

Mr. Van Hollen said the American deaths raised a broader question about Washington’s willingness to enforce its human rights laws against a close ally.

“If we can’t get accountability for them,” he said, “how are we actually implementing our human rights laws with respect to the government of Israel as it relates to the West Bank?”

“This has been building for a long time,” he added. “Enough is enough.”

item.title: Jury Begins Deliberations in Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial
item.description:
The jury began deliberations on Thursday in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman charged with murder for strangling her three young children in 2023.

After more than four weeks of testimony that was by turns emotional, harrowing and combative, the lawyers on each side made their closing arguments to the jury as to whether or not Ms. Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the children’s deaths.

At the courthouse in Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday morning, Ms. Clancy dabbed her face with a tissue as her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, described her as “a darn good mother” and a respected nurse who had loved her children.

He read from a long list of medications that had been prescribed to Ms. Clancy in the months before the killings, arguing that she received “lousy medical care” when she sought help for her anxiety, and that her mental illness had spiraled out of control.

“This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children,” Mr. Reddington said, “because she was suffering from a disease and defect.”

The judge, William Sullivan, told the jurors on Thursday morning that Ms. Clancy would not be criminally responsible if she had a mental disease or defect that prevented her from controlling her actions, or from distinguishing right from wrong.

In her closing argument, Jennifer Sprague, a prosecutor, presented the killings as a series of rational, premeditated choices, arguing that Ms. Clancy strangled the oldest children first because they were more likely to resist.

She called the killings an act of “extreme atrocity and cruelty” and described the horrific crime scene that Ms. Clancy left behind.

“She left them discarded on the basement floor, like broken toys, because she was done playing the game,” Ms. Sprague said. “You know, to a moral certainty, she is guilty.”

Ms. Clancy, 36, does not deny that she killed the children at her home in Duxbury, Mass., a Boston suburb. But Mr. Reddington has pursued an insanity defense, maintaining that she should not be held criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and had experienced auditory hallucinations that day of a man’s voice ordering her to kill her children and then herself.

Prosecutors have argued that Ms. Clancy plotted to get her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the house on Jan. 24, 2023. Mr. Clancy returned home from picking up takeout food to find the children in the basement with exercise bands around their necks, he said during his testimony. Cora, 5, and Dawson, 3, were dead. Callan, 8 months, died days later.

Mr. Clancy also found Ms. Clancy lying injured in the backyard. She had cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window of the home in what her lawyers have called a suicide attempt, which left her partially paralyzed.

Witnesses for the trial have also included Ms. Clancy’s mother, her sister and health professionals who treated Ms. Clancy before the killings or evaluated her afterward. The prosecution rested early last week after calling more than 70 witnesses, and the defense rested on Friday after calling 10.

Rebuttals, which give prosecutors an opportunity to respond to claims made by the defense, took up the last few days of the trial. The three witnesses for the prosecution, all forensic psychologists, pointed to evidence that Ms. Clancy may not have been suffering from postpartum psychosis.

The cross-examinations were combative. Mr. Reddington grilled the rebuttal witnesses and at one point asked the judge to grant a mistrial after a psychologist mentioned the concept of mortal sin while discussing Ms. Clancy’s Catholic upbringing.

On many days, demonstrators have gathered outside the courtroom. Many have been women, wearing pink to support Ms. Clancy, and to call attention to what they see as the health care system’s failure to care for new mothers with postpartum depression and other mental illnesses.

In her closing argument, Ms. Sprague said that the case was “not about our mental health system, or how it treats women.”

She added: “That’s a distraction to get you angry and passionate — about an important issue, but an issue that’s not on trial here.”

To secure a guilty verdict, the prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt not only that Ms. Clancy committed the crime, but also that she was criminally responsible for it — that she understood her actions.

Judge Sullivan also instructed the jury to choose among first-degree murder, second-degree murder and manslaughter if they find Ms. Clancy guilty. She faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder.

item.title: Starbucks Drops Drink Powder That Enveloped Baristas in Clouds of Dust
item.description:
Earlier this summer, Destiny Valencia and her fellow baristas at a Starbucks in San Jose, Calif., were learning to make a new line of specialty drinks when they began to feel sick.

The drinks, called blended refreshers, were billed as a “smooth, frozen twist” on the neon-hued, fruit-speckled iced drinks that young people posted on TikTok.

The new refreshers included an ingredient called “blending powder,” meant to preserve the drink’s slushy integrity. But as soon as Ms. Valencia started handling the powder, there was a problem: It went airborne.

“It kind of creates a smoke cloud,” Ms. Valencia said. Among her colleagues, she added, “there were thoughts of — is this OK to breathe in?”

Soon, orders were pouring in for blended mango dragonfruit lemonade refreshers and blended blue coconut lemonade refreshers. Ms. Valencia started getting headaches.

“Any time I had to use it, I had to hold my breath,” she said. Her colleagues complained about coughs and tickling throats. Baristas around the country reported developing hives and having asthma attacks.

This week, Starbucks removed the blending powder from its U.S. stores.

Jaci Anderson, a spokeswoman for the company, said blended refreshers had been removed in a regular seasonal menu transition. She said Starbucks had no plans to bring back the powder.

“Partners and customers can feel confident in the ingredients we use,” Ms. Anderson said.

Workers United, the union representing thousands of Starbucks employees at more than 700 of the nearly 17,000 Starbucks stores in the United States, called the move a victory, won through worker complaints and outraged social media posts.

“We know our collective action prompted the company to direct stores to remove the powder by the end of August,” said Jasmine Leli, a union barista and bargaining delegate from Buffalo. She said the union wanted Starbucks to consult baristas before introducing ingredients that could affect their health.

The blended refreshers are a bright, frothy reminder of the challenges Starbucks faces: tight competition for consumer attention, a protracted labor dispute and consumers more attuned to the potential health risks of food additives.

Refreshers are a fast-growing business for restaurant chains. The brightly colored, sweet drinks are showing up on menus everywhere, in a race to create unique, or bizarre, versions of the drinks to capture attention on social media and in consumers’ imaginations.

For Starbucks, refreshers are a $2-billion-a-year business and an important part of a turnaround under Brian Niccol, the chief executive, who joined the company nearly two years ago.

“Refreshers remained a standout platform for us,” Mr. Niccol said on an earnings call in July. He said the drinks had delivered double-digit annual revenue growth and encouraged customers to visit the chain throughout the day.

Refreshers and Frappuccinos, the refreshers’ increasingly elaborate elder cousins, have become the bane of existence for many baristas. Customers often request customizations that make the drinks laborious to prepare. Unless baristas add a binding agent, such as the cream used in Frappuccinos, blended drinks can separate within minutes into an unappetizing diptych of discolored ice and luminous juice.

Enter the blending powder.

It “was flying off the shelves,” said Nick Parker-Smith, a shift supervisor at a Starbucks in Springfield, Mo. He meant this figuratively and literally: The powder, he said, “becomes airborne quite easily.”

“We really weren’t equipped to handle this,” Mr. Parker-Smith added.

Baristas complained about the powder on Reddit and in social media videos, describing rashes and breathing problems, sharing ways to protect themselves from the cloud that kicked up when they used the powder, especially when it was poured into countertop containers from the plastic bags in which it arrived.

A complaint about the powder’s use at a Starbucks in Maryland was filed with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, according to the union and public records. The company said the complaint had been resolved.

Barista concerns about the powder grew when social media posts drew attention to the ingredients, which included a small amount of amorphous silica, an additive that prevents clumping and that the Food and Drug Administration has approved for consumption.

Crystalline silica, a different form of the same chemical compound, can cause a lethal lung disease, silicosis, when inhaled as a fine dust. It has been linked to a health crisis among countertop manufacturers working with artificial stone, which often contains large amounts of the material.

Amorphous silica has not been linked to the same illness, and has been proposed as an alternative to crystalline silica in countertops. But doctors generally advise against breathing any kind of dust for extended periods, at a minimum because of irritation in the airways.

Two weeks after the blended refreshers were introduced in July, Starbucks posted a note on its website saying the blending powder was safe. The company also released guidance to baristas on how to transfer the powder to the countertop containers, urging them to pour slowly.

“It’s safe for use in food and safe for use in our coffeehouses when used according to instructions,” Ms. Anderson, the Starbucks spokeswoman, said.

Workers United asked Dr. Peter Orris, an occupational health physician at the University of Illinois, for feedback. In a letter to the union reviewed by The New York Times, Dr. Orris said that the powder contained ingredients that might be deemed safe, but that Starbucks “should have evaluated it with respect to its impact on human health prior to introducing it in a setting exposing both employees and customers to the aerosolized powder through both inhalation and skin deposition.”

Dr. Orris said there appeared to be no lasting consequences to human health, aside from irritation during exposure, though the effects were worse for people with asthma or allergies.

The union sent the letter to Starbucks headquarters in Seattle.

item.title: Trump Raises Money in Texas With Control of the Senate in the Balance
item.description:
With control of the Senate hanging in the balance, President Trump is heading to Houston on Friday to raise money to help a Republican ally who has been struggling.

The Republican National Committee is holding a fund-raiser for Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general who is running for Senate. He was trailing his Democratic rival, James Talarico, in several recent polls.

Mr. Paxton prevailed in the Republican primary over Senator John Cornyn, who many analysts believe would have easily won the general election, after Mr. Trump endorsed Mr. Paxton. Mr. Trump viewed Mr. Cornyn as less than loyal after he said in 2023 that Mr. Trump’s time had “passed him by.”

But the result is that Republicans are locked in a closer-than-expected general election race that is likely to be one of the most expensive in U.S. history.

Republicans already hold 53 seats in the Senate, and this year’s election map generally favors the party. But midterm elections often represent a backlash to the party in power. The president’s approval rating is well underwater, dragged down by rising prices and an unpopular war. And Republicans have done themselves few favors with some of the candidates they advanced in their primaries.

In Texas, Mr. Paxton has been indicted on securities fraud charges (he reached a deal with prosecutors to avoid a criminal trial), has escaped an impeachment trial, has been accused of adultery by his estranged wife and was even caught on video years ago pilfering an expensive pen.

Democrats have nominated Mr. Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian who has made his Christian faith a centerpiece of his campaign. The popular podcaster Joe Rogan once told him to run for president.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, recently moved the race in Texas from the “Lean Republican” category to “Toss Up,” citing polling and the economic environment.

Many Republicans are hoping for financial support from Mr. Trump, whose fund-raising power in the party remains unmatched despite his low poll numbers. The president’s well-funded but tightfisted super PAC, MAGA Inc., came to the rescue of Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina in her hotly contested Republican runoff this week. The group flooded the contest with more than $800,000 worth of voter calls and text messages.

Republicans are now hoping for an even greater level of support for Mr. Paxton. The fund-raiser is closed to the press.

There is another motivation for Mr. Trump to get involved in the race for Congress. If Democrats take control of either chamber, they are likely to subject the president to a torrent of investigations and possible impeachment.

While in Texas, Mr. Trump also has other business. On Friday, the president will present the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the four members of the Artemis II crew, who completed a historic 10-day flight around the moon, before returning to Washington.

item.title: Trump Administration to Expand Deportation Flights to Haiti
item.description:
The Trump administration plans to step up deportation flights to Haiti, according to documents obtained by The New York Times, a move intended to more quickly expel thousands of Haitians whose legal status expired this summer with the end of a humanitarian program.

The administration aims to increase the pace of flights from once a month to once a week, the documents show, potentially allowing for the deportation of hundreds more people per month. The flights are expected to continue weekly in the near term, though a U.S. official cautioned that the plans were still being finalized.

A plane of about 57 deportees arrived in the city of Cap Haitien just before noon local time on Thursday, according to Human Rights Watch, which had personnel on hand at the airport to monitor and document the situation.

Just before the plane landed, another deportation flight arrived, this one carrying an unexpectedly large number of people who had been deported from the Bahamas. The larger surge outstripped the ability of the Haitian migration agency and the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration to receive them, said Nathalye Cotrino, a senior researcher for Human Rights Watch, who was at the airport.

“For now, the U.S. deportees are waiting in a tent,” Ms. Cotrino said. “People arrived very confused and upset, and a few were aggressive, so it is a delicate situation to manage.”

Bill O’Neill, the United Nations’ human rights expert for Haiti, said the massive influx of deportees in a single day was unmanageable.

“This is insane. There is no way the Haitian government can handle this,” he said. “There is nowhere for these people to go.”

Mr. O’Neill said a massacre this week in Kenscoff, outside the capital of Port-au-Prince, underscores how dangerous the situation is. “No country should be forcing Haitians to return to Haiti, because there is no guarantee of a safe, dignified and sustainable return to the country,” he said.

The push to expel Haitians illegally in the United States comes after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in June that the administration was free to end Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status, a program that blocks the deportation of people from designated countries deemed too dangerous to accept its citizens. The Trump administration concluded that Haiti is safe enough to be removed from the protected list, despite widespread lawlessness and gang activity in the country.

The State Department has warned U.S. travelers not to visit Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care.” The Federal Aviation Administration banned commercial airlines from landing in Port-au-Prince earlier this year, citing “ongoing instability.” There have been reports of gangs firing on aircraft trying to land at the Port-au-Prince airport.

“There is not even a vestige of a state in control,” said Daniel Foote, the Biden administration’s special envoy to Haiti, who resigned in 2021 over the deportations of Haitian migrants. Mr. Foote, who remains in contact with people on the ground in Haiti, said the deportations would likely include many Haitian immigrants who have spent most of their lives in the United States and will now be sent to a dangerous environment.

“Not only has it not gotten better, it hasn’t stabilized,” Mr. Foote said. “It just continues to get worse and worse and worse.”

Mr. Foote questioned how the Trump administration assessed that Haiti was now safe enough for an increase of deportations. In fact, internal emails and documents obtained by The Times indicate that the Homeland Security Department decided to terminate the protections in June 2025 without obtaining input from the State Department, which typically is responsible for assessing the conditions in foreign countries.

Deporting hundreds more to Haiti will hasten deportations, but it will still take time to reach the more than 300,000 Haitians who had been allowed to legally live and work in the United States under the expired protected status. The administration will most likely need to further increase the pace to expel every Haitian now in the country illegally. The administration has offered people in the country illegally a plane ticket and $2,600 in cash to self-deport using an app.

“The federal courts have ordered the Haitian illegals must leave the U.S. and we have generously made free flights available,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, who declined to provide specific details on deportation flights to Haiti.

Seeking safer ways to land aircraft than arriving at Port-au-Prince, U.S. officials have flown migrants about 120 miles away to Cap Haitien, which is where the new flights will land. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been flying Haitians to the much smaller city once a month, according to Savi Arvey, the director of policy for immigration issues at Human Rights First, who oversees a project that tracks the deportation flights.

Last Thursday, ICE said it deported more than 160 Haitians to Cap Haitien. In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security, which houses ICE, pointed to more than a dozen Haitians on the flight with criminal records. The last deportation flight before that one was in July, according to Ms. Arvey.

The journey from Cap Haitien to Port-au-Prince used to be a six-hour drive, but it is now considered extremely unsafe. Gangs control the main highway connecting the two cities, extracting tolls and sometimes kidnapping the passengers. Deportees stranded in Cap Haitien may choose to stay there, as the northern part of the country is safer.

The United Nations said 3,050 people were killed in Haiti during the first six months of 2026. Much of that violence is centered in Port-au-Prince and the surrounding area. Dozens were killed this week alone in Kenscoff, an upper-class community on the outskirts of the capital.

About 1.5 million people have fled their homes for other cities, and nearly 250,000 people in Haiti’s capital are living in displacement camps, such as public schools and government buildings.

Temporary Protected Status “was never designed to be permanent, yet previous administrations have used it as a de facto amnesty program for decades,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement this week. “Under the strong leadership of President Donald J. Trump, we are putting America first again.”

The agency said it would not confirm future deportation flights for security reasons.

Temporary Protected Status was first offered to Haitians during the Obama administration after a devastating earthquake struck the country. The Biden administration extended the protections because of gang violence and instability in the country. But Mr. Trump has made it clear he wants to purge people from Haiti, which he disparaged as a “shithole” country even as his administration has deemed it safe for deportations.

ICE officials have called Haitian immigrants to check in in recent weeks and placed ankle monitors on them, according to advocates. The technology allows ICE officials to monitor their whereabouts.

Mr. Mullin has been under intensifying pressure by supporters of the Trump administration to ramp up deportations of Haitians. “We are giving them an opportunity to either leave on their own and we’ll help you, or we’ll arrest you and send you back,” Mr. Mullin told News Nation this month.

Top administration officials, including Stephen Miller, have said before that removing Haitians is an appropriate action.

“Well, of course, if you no longer have status in this country, then you’re supposed to be deported,” he told reporters in June.

item.title: Secrecy in Lawsuits Has ‘Run Amok,’ Scholars Say
item.description:
To hear federal appeals courts tell it, sealed filings should be exceptionally rare — and for good reason.

“Legal arguments, and the documents underlying them, belong in the public domain,” Judge Don Willett wrote for the Fifth Circuit in 2021. “American courts are not private tribunals summoned to resolve disputes confidentially at taxpayer expense.”

Countless appeals courts have agreed, insisting that judicial records are presumptively open and that sealing them requires a very good reason. Trial judges must carefully review materials that parties want to file under seal, those rulings have said, and give a detailed explanation if they decide to withhold them from public view.

But the reality on the ground, two recent studies demonstrate, is starkly different.

One study, from scholars at Stanford and Berkeley who explored data from more than two million federal civil cases, sounded an alarm about “a sealing system run amok.”

“Our findings are startling — and directly refute the notion that sealing practices are operating as designed,” the study’s authors wrote.

They found that judges granted around 90 percent of motions to seal documents. “Dozens of experienced federal judges,” they found, “granted every single sealing request they encountered.”

Relying on data gathered by Reuters for a 2019 investigation of secrecy in federal civil litigation, they found that more than 5,700 cases each year included sealed documents.

The second study, from Elizabeth Rowe, a law professor at the University of Virginia, found that efforts to seal documents have not abated. She identified more than 33,000 motions to seal in the five-year period ending in 2023.

“It’s become quite a problem,” she told me. “A lot of people don’t know the scale and the scope of what’s happening.

The root of the problem may be the adversary system. Judges are used to resolving disputes between the parties, but the parties often agree to secrecy, either expressly or tacitly.

Both studies found that more than 84 percent of motions to seal were agreed to or, more often, uncontested by the other side. Put another way, there was no one arguing on behalf of the public’s right of access.

It thus falls to trial judges to protect the public’s interest in openness, but busy judges apparently don’t always do so.

There are valid reasons to seal some filings, of course. Trade secrets, authentic national security concerns and medical records come to mind. But parties often seek to seal information that will do no more than embarrass them or, worse, hide dangers to public health and safety.

“We can have a debate about the amount of secrecy that is optimal,” Nora Freeman Engstrom, a law professor at Stanford and an author of the first study, told me. “There are all sorts of difficult trade-offs.”

But she added that judges need to do more than rubber-stamp motions to seal the materials that will form the basis of their decisions.

This is not a partisan issue. Perhaps the best recent articulation of what is at stake came from Judge Willett, a Trump appointee.

“When it comes to protecting the right of access, the judge is the public interest’s principal champion,” he wrote. “And when the parties are mutually interested in secrecy, the judge is its only champion.”

Years ago, when I practiced law in the corporate legal department of The New York Times Company, I observed the same thing in litigating challenges to sealed dockets in terrorism cases. Judges would ultimately follow the law, but only after an outsider — usually a news outlet — objected.

“The rights at stake are those of the public,” I wrote in 2000 in The Journal of Law and Policy. “And the public should not have to rely on a newspaper’s decision to allocate resources to the vindication of the public’s rights. The responsibility for the enforcement of the public’s procedural rights is lodged with the judiciary itself.”

Professor Engstrom’s study and my article both included a quotation from a 1980 opinion by Chief Justice Warren Burger.

“People in an open society do not demand infallibility from their institutions,” he wrote, “but it is difficult for them to accept what they are prohibited from observing.”

A 15-year-old fell asleep during a field trip to a Detroit courthouse while a judge talked about his career. The judge, Kenneth King, according to the student’s lawsuit, responded by ordering her to be detained for hours in a holding cell, handcuffed, dressed in a jail jumpsuit and subjected to a fake trial streamed on the internet during which he threatened to send her to “juvie,” scaring her with, as the lawsuit put it, “vulgar stories of beatings and feces.” The Sixth Circuit last week rejected Judge King’s argument that his conduct was entitled to absolute judicial immunity and allowed her lawsuit to proceed.

Nicholas Casey was able to contact migrants deported from the United States to Eswatini, a tiny country in southern Africa where they may be held for the rest of their lives. In an article and a video for The New York Times Magazine, Casey illuminates the human cost and questionable legality of “third-country deportations.”

Mailbag

We’ve gotten a bunch of questions from confused readers about the brief order Chief Justice John Roberts issued on Friday letting President Trump keep working on his 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom while the full court decides how to handle the issue.

I asked my colleague Ann Marimow, who covers the Supreme Court, to clear things up. Here’s Ann:

The confusion came in part because the chief justice acted on his own, in a one-sentence order known as an “administrative stay.” The chief justice did not include any reasoning or a timeline for the court’s next steps, saying only that it would be in place “pending further order of the undersigned or of the court.”

Why didn’t the full court act? And what did this say about the fate of the ballroom project?

To start, Chief Justice Roberts handles emergency requests from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which ruled that the president had exceeded his authority by trying to build the ballroom without congressional approval.

He can handle emergency requests from the circuit on his own. But ordinarily, he would refer any matter of significance to all nine justices for consideration.

We do know the court was facing a deadline. The appeals court had paused its order blocking construction — but only until Friday. Had the court done nothing, it would have taken effect.

So Chief Justice Roberts’s one-line action, paired with the suggestion that something more is likely to come from the court but without a specified timeline, may indicate the nine justices are struggling to reach consensus about how to proceed in a more lasting way.

The court has never publicly defined the standards it relies on when issuing administrative stays, so we can’t wager any guesses about why the chief justice thought one was appropriate here.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett, joined by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, provided some insight in a 2024 case into how she thinks about placeholder “administrative stays” issued by lower courts.

The orders, she wrote, “do not typically reflect the court’s consideration” of the underlying merits of a request, but rather freeze legal proceedings. At the same time, she wrote, just because such orders are described as administrative, “does not mean they are value neutral.”

The point is to “minimize harm,” she wrote, and the choice “reflects a first-blush judgment about the relative consequences” of pausing a lower-court ruling versus allowing it to take effect.

By allowing construction to proceed, the chief justice’s order seemed to suggest he might agree with the Trump administration’s assertion that halting the project, which includes a secure military bunker underneath, would do more harm than not. The government told the court that construction is proceeding 20 hours a day, seven days a week with a crew of 250 workers, and that stopping work now would put the president and his family at risk.

The preservationists challenging the project have said the administration’s assertions are just an effort to complete the project before the court can weigh in and essentially “outrun judicial review.”

Ann and I would love to hear your questions on the law, the courts or whatever is on your mind. Send them my way at the-docket@nytimes.com.

Closing Argument

Three years after President Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 as calls for his impeachment over his role in the Watergate scandal grew, he made a memorable statement in a television interview. “When the president does it,” he told David Frost, “that means that it is not illegal.”

I knew about Nixon’s assertion, but I had no idea that he had gone on to publish a long essay in The Washington Star explaining what he had meant. The essay was the subject of a fascinating post on Friday by Michael Dreeben on Just Security, a legal policy blog. Dreeben is a veteran of the solicitor general’s office who has argued more than 100 cases in the Supreme Court.

Plainly stung by the biting criticism his comment had provoked, Nixon provided a lucid, cogent but, in my view, not especially convincing account of presidential power. He insisted that he did not believe that presidents were entirely above the law, and that he had meant only that they had wide latitude in addressing emergencies.

Nixon was a lawyer, and his tone was lawyerly. But his core claim was bold.

“He is not an autocrat,” Nixon wrote of the president. “He does not rule by fiat. His powers are not unlimited. But neither can he be powerless to go beyond the strict letter of existing law — in a limited way, and at times of special need.”

Dreeben’s most recent appearance before the justices was for the government in Trump v. United States in 2024. That was the case in which the court granted presidents substantial immunity from prosecution.

Nixon was pardoned and so never faced prosecution. Under the reasoning of the court’s decision in the immunity case, the pardon may well have been unnecessary.

In his post, Dreeben said he heard an echo.

“The Nixon and Trump presidencies are eerily similar,” he wrote. Both presidents were at war with the federal bureaucracy, with journalists and with other perceived enemies, Dreeben said, adding that he believed both had misused the I.R.S. and the Department of Justice.

But Nixon, Dreeben wrote, “could only have dreamed about the power that Trump has flexed.”

As for Nixon’s famous assertion, it was not so very different from one that Trump posted on social media last year: “He who saves his Country does not violate any law.”

item.title: DeSantis Administration Misspent $10 Million, Grand Jury Says
item.description:
Gov. Ron DeSantis’s administration “misappropriated” $10 million in taxpayer money by diverting it to a charity tied to his wife, according to a leaked Florida grand jury report that took a sharply critical view of the dealings.

The report also said grand jurors found insufficient evidence to levy charges. But it intensified a controversy over the investigation into the fund-raising arm of Hope Florida, the charity that the first lady, Casey DeSantis, started in 2021. The charity’s goal is to keep families off public assistance by connecting them with churches and aid groups.

In 2024, the charity’s fund-raising arm, the Hope Florida Foundation, received $10 million from a state Medicaid settlement. It was quickly redirected to political committees backing a campaign led by the governor against a ballot measure that would have legalized marijuana.

The transactions amounted to misuse of public funds as “part of a sophisticated scheme to fund political activities,” the grand jury found in its report, which was published online by CBS News Miami on Wednesday. The report was completed in January but has been kept secret since.

The New York Times could not independently verify the document, but none of the officials named in it have questioned its veracity. Instead, they have decried that the report was leaked despite still being under court seal.

Asked about the report at an event on Thursday, Mr. DeSantis called its finding that funds were misappropriated “a lie.”

“Obviously, there was a crime committed to leak it,” he told reporters in Lake City, Fla., about the report.

The matter involved key figures in Florida’s state government, and the resulting scandal hurt both Mr. and Ms. DeSantis politically. Ms. DeSantis had made the Hope Florida initiative central to her public persona; it was seen as a potential launchpad for a campaign to succeed her term-limited husband. In the end, she did not run, and Mr. DeSantis, a Republican, did not endorse anyone in the G.O.P. primary for governor.

According to the report, several witnesses said that they could not recall who directed the $10 million to go to the Hope Florida Foundation.

“While we can’t prove who is responsible,” the report said, “we can plainly see that taxpayer money was misused for political purposes, and we would like to see changes made to prevent this from happening again.”

Prosecutors impanel grand juries to hear witness testimony and determine whether there is enough evidence for a criminal indictment. While grand juries in Florida are secret, their reports are typically made public, even if they reach conclusions other than an indictment.

People named in such reports may ask a judge to keep them secret. It is unclear if that is why this report has remained under seal.

Jack Campbell, the Democratic state attorney for Leon County, which includes Tallahassee, the capital, impaneled the grand jury. In March, he declined to comment on the existence of the report. On Thursday, his office reiterated in a statement that “the records are confidential as part of an investigation.”

The outcome of the investigation was not unusual in a case involving government deals, said Joseph M. Centorino, a former public corruption prosecutor in Miami who was not involved in the investigation. Proving criminal intent is difficult when multiple government officials — especially lawyers — previously approved a suspicious deal, he said.

“People relying on the advice of attorneys provides a built-in defense” in such cases, he said.

James Uthmeier, who was Mr. DeSantis’s chief of staff at the time and is now the state’s Republican attorney general, was central to the transactions investigated by the grand jury. Also involved, though less directly, was Ashley Moody, who was then the attorney general and is now the state’s junior Republican U.S. senator.

Both Mr. Uthmeier and Ms. Moody were appointed by Mr. DeSantis and now are seeking to be elected on their own merits in November. Both have denied wrongdoing.

“The reports confirm what we have said all along,” Will O’Grady, a spokesman for Ms. Moody, said in a statement on Wednesday. He added: “Neither the Department of Legal Affairs nor the former attorney general had knowledge of how the settlement money would be spent. Attempts to characterize this any other way are disingenuous.”

Asked about the report at an event on Thursday, Mr. Uthmeier said he was not allowed to talk about it. He suggested without evidence that Democrats had been behind the leaked report.

Mr. Uthmeier also called the investigation a “hoax.”

“Nobody did anything wrong here,” he told reporters in The Villages, Fla. “There was not even probable cause to move forward.”

Democrats seized on the report, with Mr. Uthmeier’s and Ms. Moody’s election rivals calling for their resignations. David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor, said he would pursue reopening the investigation if he were elected.

The investigation centered on a $10 million payment that the Hope Florida Foundation received in 2024 from Centene, a Medicaid contractor that had overbilled and settled with the DeSantis administration. The grand jury found that Ms. Moody’s office knew of the payment and that her chief deputy at the time approved it “without conducting his due diligence to ensure the proper appropriation of taxpayer funds.”

Before 2024, the Hope Florida Foundation had raised only about $2 million over three years.

Soon after receiving the $10 million windfall, the foundation distributed it to two nonprofit political committees known as “dark money” groups, which do not have to release detailed financial reports. The groups then routed $8.5 million to Keep Florida Clean, a political action committee created to oppose legalized marijuana.

Then, Keep Florida Clean sent $10.5 million to the Republican Party of Florida and $1.1 million to the Florida Freedom Fund, Mr. DeSantis’s PAC. Both those groups also spent money opposing the marijuana measure. Although most voters supported the amendment in November 2024, it failed to get the 60 percent of votes needed to pass.

At the time, Mr. Uthmeier ran both Keep Florida Clean and the Florida Freedom Fund.

The report found that Mr. Uthmeier “was in a position of authority over those involved in settling” with Centene and that witnesses identified him “as having involvement” in directing the money after it went to the foundation.

But the report noted that no witnesses had admitted directing the money to go to the foundation in the first place, or identified who did.

item.title: C.I.A. Chief Delivered Bleak Assessment of Russia’s War in Secretive Moscow Visit
item.description:
John Ratcliffe, the C.I.A. director, made a secretive visit to Moscow this week to privately share his bleak assessment of the state of the Russian war against Ukraine, and to urge the Russians to cut a deal before their military and economic situation gets worse, current and former officials said.

Mr. Ratcliffe delivered the message to Aleksandr V. Bortnikov, the head of Russia’s F.S.B. intelligence service, and made no threats about potential consequences for the Russian side should President Vladimir V. Putin ignore the C.I.A. director’s assessment and choose to continue fighting.

C.I.A. analysts have long questioned whether Mr. Putin’s advisers have given him honest assessments of the war’s trajectory and toll.

The C.I.A. has long maintained communications channels with the F.S.B. and Russia’s foreign intelligence service, which is known as the S.V.R.

Officials said Mr. Ratcliffe’s intelligence channel with Bortnikov runs parallel to separate channels that President Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, have established with other senior advisers to Mr. Putin.

Some officials said they hoped that Mr. Putin, a former intelligence officer himself, would see a message from the C.I.A. director as more urgent and credible than communications through normal diplomatic channels.

For much of last year, Mr. Trump and some of his top advisers appeared to hold the belief that a Russian battlefield victory over Ukraine was inevitable because of Russia’s larger population and its nuclear arsenal.

But the Russians have suffered massive losses, and their battlefield gains have stalled.

It is not clear whether Mr. Ratcliffe’s message presaged any change in U.S. policy toward Russia or Ukraine.

Mr. Ratcliffe’s visit was the latest effort by the Trump administration to breathe new life into stalled negotiations. It has become increasingly clear that Ukraine is not going to give up its fight in the east, even with reduced U.S. military support.

Given what he presented as the bleak military and economic reality for Russia, Mr. Ratcliffe told Mr. Bortnikov that he believed it was time for Moscow to engage in serious negotiations to end the war.

Since Mr. Trump’s return to office, the United States has scaled back its military support to the Ukrainians, forcing them to rely more heavily on European partners.

The C.I.A. has maintained its close intelligence partnerships with the Ukrainians, which began more than a decade ago.

The private message that Mr. Ratcliffe delivered to Mr. Bortnikov about Ukraine echoed some of the director’s public statements.

Last month, Mr. Ratcliffe spoke out pointedly about Russian troop losses during the war, and Moscow’s inability to advance on the battlefield. He noted that the life expectancy of a Russian soldier on the front lines was less than 35 minutes.

And he added that Russia had gained only about 1 percent of Ukraine’s total territory in the 18 months since he became C.I.A. director, a development he attributed to Ukraine’s “mastery” of drone technology.

Before Mr. Ratcliffe met with Mr. Bortnikov in Moscow, he spoke with his Ukrainian counterparts, assuring them that he would be exploring Russian positions, not making concessions on behalf of the Ukrainians.

European diplomats believe there may be an opening to secure a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine in the coming winter months, given the largely stalled Russian offensive in the Donbas, and because of Ukraine’s ability to continue imposing deep costs on Russia with its drone warfare.

Some of those European officials have been pressing the Trump administration to add a national security official to the mix of officials pressing the Russians for a peace deal, someone who could deliver the kind of tough message Mr. Ratcliffe delivered this week.

The Ukrainians have long viewed Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner as too close to the Russians. They view Mr. Ratcliffe, a longtime Russia hawk, as a potentially more neutral mediator.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly used Mr. Ratcliffe as a discreet messenger.

In January, he became the first cabinet-level official to visit Venezuela after U.S. special operation forces seized President Nicolás Maduro.

In May, he traveled to Cuba, giving its leaders a bleak assessment of the state of the Cuban economy in the face of a U.S. oil blockade. He urged the country to make a series of sweeping political and economic changes before the situation got worse.

Direct contacts between U.S. and Russian spy chiefs have been sporadic in recent years.

In November 2021, William J. Burns, the C.I.A. director in the Biden administration, met face to face in Moscow with Mr. Bortnikov and other top Russian officials to warn Mr. Putin against launching a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A year later, in November 2022, Turkey hosted a face-to-face meeting in Ankara between Mr. Burns and Sergei Naryshkin, the leader of Russia’s foreign intelligence service. U.S. intelligence agencies had intercepted Russian communications about the possible use of a nuclear device by the Russians to slow Ukrainian advances in that fall’s counteroffensive. Mr. Burns warned Mr. Naryshkin of serious consequences if the Russians acted on the alleged threat.

The Turkish hosts wanted the meeting to be the start of a lasting channel of direct communication between Washington and Moscow to reduce tensions. But the C.I.A. was angry at Moscow when, after the meeting, the Russian side made it public. Mr. Burns and Mr. Naryshkin did not have a second face-to-face meeting, though they continued to communicate occasionally by phone.

After Mr. Trump took office last year, Mr. Ratcliffe and Mr. Bortnikov worked out the details of a prisoner swap, but this week’s face-to-face meeting in Moscow was their first.

item.title: Trump Orders the Government to Rename Lake Ontario to Lake America
item.description:
President Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, carrying out his threat to rename the easternmost Great Lake as part of an escalating trade war with Canada.

During remarks in the Oval Office, Mr. Trump said that the order, which directs the Interior Department to update the government’s Geographic Names Information System to reflect the name change, was effective immediately.

After signing the order, Mr. Trump reiterated his criticism that Canada had been taking advantage of the United States, and that the country “treats us very badly.” He added that Canada was the “worst” to deal with on trade, and he reissued his threat to impose steep tariffs on automobiles made there.

“Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly,” he said. “Even the military, you know, we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything.”

Canada, like the United States, is part of NATO, a security alliance with a mutual defense agreement. Canada is also one of the United States’ closest intelligence partners.

Like Mr. Trump’s order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, Thursday’s order most likely requires only federal entities to recognize the change, but it does not have to be recognized by other countries. Mr. Trump told reporters that the administration had “filed all the necessary papers, documents” and “notified all of the various people that we have to notify” to make the change.

“So we’ve done everything that you have to do,” he said, “and this is official, effective immediately.”

Canadian and American officials have both rebuffed Mr. Trump’s attempt to rename the body of water.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul dismissed Mr. Trump’s threat earlier this week as “silly talk.” And on Thursday, she reposted the White House’s new directive on social media, and said the state, which borders the lake, will not comply. “New York won’t be calling it that,” she wrote.

Wab Kinew, the premier of Manitoba, likened Mr. Trump’s actions to a has-been rock group replaying songs from their heyday.

“He thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico, and he’s trying to bring that back,” Mr. Kinew told reporters on Thursday afternoon. “He’s trying to play the hits for his base, but I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney also weighed in, saying in a social media post: “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Mr. Trump first announced in a social media post earlier this week that the United States was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario after trade talks between the two countries fell apart.

Canadian officials walked away from what they publicly described as deal-breaking demands from the United States. In the social media post, Mr. Trump said that the name change was being considered because “we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

Mr. Trump then continued to troll Canada on Wednesday by posting a photo of a map with Lake Ontario crossed out in red ink, and a video of him swiping through the name with a pen and writing “Lake America” in its place.

On Thursday, Mr. Trump displayed a large poster board depicting the new “Lake America” that blared “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater.”

Vjosa Isai contributed from Toronto.

item.title: Obama to Headline Fund-Raiser With Jeffries in New York
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama will headline a fund-raiser for House Democrats on Sept. 10 in New York with Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, as Democrats try to restock their political war chest before the final sprint to the fall midterm elections.

Mr. Obama is set to attend a reception and dinner, with proceeds going to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, according to a copy of the invitation obtained by The New York Times.

The dinner is set for the second night of Republicans’ unusual two-day midterm convention in Dallas, which President Trump pushed for as an effort to mobilize his party’s voters. But the Democratic fund-raiser in New York is not necessarily counterprogramming: Two people familiar with the plans, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the private event, said that Mr. Obama’s appearance was expected to be entirely behind closed doors.

“House Democrats are grateful for President Barack Obama’s strong support in our effort to take back the House,” Justin Chermol, a spokesman for Mr. Jeffries, said in a statement. He said Democrats would be focused on their affordability agenda “while MAGA extremists celebrate the failures of Republican-controlled government at their so-called midterm convention.”

Money is a top concern for Democrats headed into the fall. The leading Republican committees, especially the Republican National Committee, have far more cash on hand than their Democratic counterparts. And President Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., which has yet to reveal its midterm spending plans, has more than $400 million in the bank.

The D.C.C.C., House Democrats’ campaign arm, entered August with $80.2 million in its treasury, compared with $92.4 million for the National Republican Congressional Committee. All told, the D.C.C.C. has raised slightly more money this election cycle.

Mr. Obama remains one of the Democratic Party’s most desired surrogates and powerful fund-raisers. He is set to headline another fund-raiser in the coming days on Martha’s Vineyard for the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, which plays a key role in the fight over gerrymandered congressional maps.

Mr. Obama has begun more public political engagements, as well, recently recording a video playing basketball with the Democratic nominee for Senate in Iowa, Josh Turek, who was a two-time Paralympic gold medalist on the U.S. men’s wheelchair basketball team.

Mr. Obama also made an appearance in Texas to buy tacos with James Talarico, the state’s Democratic nominee for Senate. And the former president called Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s nominee in Michigan, after a divisive primary, as well as his primary rival, Representative Haley Stevens.

Mr. Obama previously headlined a fund-raiser with Mr. Jeffries in late 2025 in the Los Angeles area. One person familiar with the event said it had raised $2 million.

item.title: In Trump’s Washington, Ballooning National Debt Stirs Little Action
item.description:
It used to be that a new report of budgetary red ink would touch off a political crisis in Washington. There would be speeches and news conferences and blue-ribbon commissions and legislation and brinkmanship over how to get the nation’s fiscal house in order.

But when the national debt topped $40 trillion last week — that’s trillion with a T — the collective body politic all but shrugged. Never mind that the U.S. government now owes twice as much money as a share of the economy than two decades ago. Republicans and Democrats issued perfunctory, my-we’re-concerned statements and promptly moved on.

The bond markets were not so sanguine, as a sell-off indicated, but the relative indifference in the nation’s capital demonstrated how drastically the politics of deficit spending has changed in recent years. For generations, the nation’s fiscal imbalance was a constant preoccupation of presidents and members of Congress, a defining issue that shaped the rest of their agendas. Now it seems to be barely an afterthought as Washington borrows heavily to finance tax cuts and spending programs.

Both parties are engaged in a kind of conspiracy of silence about the eye-watering numbers, preferring to concentrate on other issues, whether it be the Iran war or the cost of living. President Trump is busy trying to restrict mail-in voting in the midterm elections and build his ballroom. Democrats are busy tying Republican opponents to an unpopular president in hopes of taking back one or both houses of Congress.

It has been 15 years since the last time Washington engaged in a serious bipartisan effort to curb the deficit, and both political polarization and government indebtedness have only grown exponentially since then. Few think that today’s leaders would or could come together anytime soon to make the hard choices, compromises and sacrifices that analysts say are necessary.

“The fiscal situation has never been worse and yet the political situation has never been worse and so we are absolutely unable to meet the moment,” said Maya MacGuineas, the president of the bipartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, one of the few institutions in Washington that still consistently focuses attention on deficit spending.

“The political norm was as soon as you passed some line where things started to feel worrisome, everyone would put on their grown-up pants and do some of the hard work of being political leaders,” she said. “And that’s just not the case anymore.”

Erskine B. Bowles, who led a bipartisan commission to tame deficit spending in 2010, said leaders in both parties these days are applying “the ostrich theory” to the issue, putting their heads in the sand. “They get the arithmetic,” he said. “They understand that we have a dysfunctional government, that we’re addicted to debt, that we have these $2 trillion deficits as far as the eye can see. And we don’t have a plan to deal with it.”

The only real reaction from Mr. Trump’s administration came from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who tried to settle the bond markets with a debt buyback plan that failed to reassure investors and was derided even by his mentor, the hedge fund billionaire Stanley F. Druckenmiller. In the long run, Mr. Bessent’s stated prescription for the sky-high deficits was to say that “we’re going to have to grow our way out of this.” That is a hope, not a plan, and one that would require the kind of sustained economic growth not seen in decades.

The government is set to spend $1.9 trillion more than it takes in this fiscal year, or 5.8 percent of the entire economy, according to the Congressional Budget Office. That gap is projected to grow to $3.1 trillion, or 6.7 percent, by 2036. Debt held by the public already equals 101 percent of the American economy and at this rate will grow to 120 percent in 2036, surpassing the record of 106 percent just after World War II. The government now spends more on interest payments than on the Pentagon budget.

Both parties have contributed to the gap over the years through tax cuts and spending programs that appealed to voters. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. pushed through an expansive economic stimulus package after the Covid-19 pandemic as well as legislation to finance roads, bridges and other infrastructure and to invest in climate change, semiconductors and other priorities. Mr. Trump has enacted large tax reductions while pushing for a vast increase in military spending.

While the conservative House Freedom Caucus has noisily tried to use government shutdowns or debt ceiling fights to force major spending cuts, neither Mr. Biden nor Mr. Trump devoted much energy to finding a way to bring the books closer to balance. Nor did they pay a political price, reflecting a new reality when it comes to deficits. During Mr. Trump’s first term, Mick Mulvaney, while his acting chief of staff, reportedly told supporters of the president that “nobody cares” about the deficit anymore.

That may not be exactly true but it is not quite as high on the voters’ priority list. Fifty percent of Americans said they cared about the deficit “a great deal” in March, down from 64 percent in 2011, according to Gallup surveys. Only 2 percent of voters think the deficit or debt is the most important problem facing the country today, according to Gallup.

On the other hand, the Pew Research Center found that those who consider the deficit a “very big problem for the country today” has swelled from 55 percent in 2018 to 64 percent this year. Taken together, the surveys seem to suggest that voters believe it is an issue but do not care as much as they once did.

Stephanie Kelton, a former chief economist for Democrats on the Senate Budget Committee, said Americans had grown inured to doomsday predictions that did not materialize. “It’s just a running, century-long commentary where there’s always an iceberg or a giant dinosaur or a cancer eating you, gobbling you, terrifying you,” she said. “But nothing bad has happened. You would think if it was going to happen, it would have happened by now.”

That represents a profound change in Washington, where for years the deficit dominated politics. President Ronald Reagan was elected in 1980 in part on the issue, but his tax cuts and military buildup only increased the deficit, forcing him to reverse course and raise some taxes again. President George H.W. Bush was so concerned about the deficit that he broke his “no new taxes” campaign vow and negotiated a package of increases and spending cuts with Democrats that helped doom his re-election in 1992.

President Bill Clinton pushed through his own politically risky deficit plan with tax increases and spending reductions, relying entirely on Democratic votes, which propelled Republicans in taking over Congress in 1994 elections. But in his second term, buoyed in part by strong economic growth, Mr. Clinton and Mr. Bowles, his chief of staff, brokered a deal with Speaker Newt Gingrich that finally balanced the budget.

The brief surpluses turned back to deficits under President George W. Bush thanks to his tax cuts, a recession and national security spending prompted by the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Mr. Bush invested hundreds of billions of dollars to stanch the financial crisis of 2008, although the government recouped most of that. President Barack Obama spent hundreds of billions more to stimulate the economy.

Mr. Obama was the last president to make a serious effort to control the deficit, appointing a commission led by Mr. Bowles and Alan K. Simpson, a former Republican senator from Wyoming, who developed a painful menu of spending cuts and tax increases. It was too much for Mr. Obama, and his own negotiations for a “grand bargain” with Speaker John A. Boehner later collapsed.

Mr. Trump, who was such a prolific borrower as a private businessman that he termed himself “the king of debt,” has never seemed to care much about deficit spending. During his 2016 campaign, he almost offhandedly boasted that he could eliminate not just the deficit but the entire cumulative national debt in eight years as president. Instead, the debt has doubled since then under him and Mr. Biden.

Mr. Trump never mentioned the deficit as a priority in any of his State of the Union addresses in his first term, unlike every president since Harry S. Truman, according to a database search. In his second term, he talked about stopping wasteful spending and empowered Elon Musk to find it. Mr. Musk, who initially promised to cut $2 trillion in spending for Mr. Trump, managed $200 billion in savings, then gave up.

The lack of alarm at the latest debt numbers suggests that budget doves have gained traction in the perennial debate over deficit spending. For years, some economists have argued that deficits are not necessarily bad and can even benefit the economy.

Ms. Kelton, now a professor of economics and public policy at Stony Brook University and author of “The Deficit Myth,” is a leading champion of Modern Monetary Theory, which holds that if a government issues its own currency, it can always create money if needed to take care of its people.

A deficit on the government side, she said, means a surplus in the private sector, which can be good for the economy. The real restraint on spending, she said, should not be matching it to incoming revenue but making sure that the government does not pump so much additional money into the economy that it generates inflation.

Mr. Mulvaney’s comment that no one cared about deficits anymore, she said, “felt like a sea change to me” in terms of the perspective of the nation’s leadership. “I would like to believe there’s been some learning along the way and that people have come to understand that the thing we call the government deficit has another side to it. Too often we only present half the story.”

But deficit hawks argue that soaring government debt results in higher interest rates, which make it harder to take out a car loan or a home mortgage.

“We’re spending a trillion dollars a year on interest,” former Senator Rob Portman, a Republican of Ohio who served as the younger Mr. Bush’s budget director, said in an interview. “It’s crazy. Almost 20 cents of every dollar you send to Uncle Sam is interest now. It’s gotten to the point that it’s crowding out other priorities of the American people. We haven’t done a good job explaining that.”

Despite the restrained response to the latest debt numbers, Mr. Portman said he sees signs that people are taking the situation seriously and he has been trying to generate interest through symposia, panels, hearings and other efforts.

“I think there’s a little bit of a groundswell now to do something,” he said. “It isn’t going to be easy, it never is. But even kicking off some sort of process is important.”

Dylan Freedman contributed reporting.
