item.title: Fired Journalists at Independent Military Publication Sue Pentagon
item.description:
Three journalists at the federally funded but independent Stars and Stripes news organization sued the government on Thursday, claiming that the Pentagon fired them in retaliation for writing about the worsening conditions inside a Navy aircraft carrier deployed to the Middle East.

The journalists accused the government of violating their First Amendment right to free speech, asking the U.S. District Court in Washington to reject their terminations as well as new Pentagon policies that they say severely limit the editorial independence of their work.

The lawsuit is the latest in a streak of public pushbacks against the Pentagon’s efforts to exert control over the storied newspaper, which started publishing during the Civil War and has had a long history of independent reporting.

The publication has reported extensively on difficulties faced by military communities as the war in Iran has dragged on. The challenged terminations were first discussed a day after Stars and Stripes journalists reported on hardships that Navy sailors were facing on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, the aircraft carrier whose deployment was extended to nine months, according to the complaint. President Trump has denied reporting on the carrier’s troubles from Stars and Stripes and other news outlets as “fake news.”

The lawsuit “seeks to prevent the blatant violation of the First Amendment rights of these journalists and challenges the U.S. Department of Defense’s extraordinary censorship efforts,” the three journalists said in the complaint.

The Department of Defense declined to comment. Capt. William Urban, who became the military deputy to Stars and Stripes’ publisher earlier this month, said in a letter published last week that his priority was to ensure “the highest quality of editorially independent reporting.” Captain Urban had previously served as a senior spokesman for the Defense Department and NATO.

Captain Urban told senior leadership at Stars at Stripes last week that he would eventually assume the role as the publisher, according to an official who is not authorized to speak about the matter.

For months, the Defense Department has faced public disagreements on its new operations policy on Stars and Stripes from the news outlet’s members.

In June, the newspaper’s editorial watchdog, Jacqueline Smith, filed a lawsuit after being fired, which she attributed to having publicly criticized the Pentagon leadership for editorial interference. Several members of the publisher’s advisory board also sued the Defense Department that month for adopting policies that banned Stars and Stripes from publishing comics and wire reprints.

In July, CBS News interviewed the paper’s editor in chief, Erik A. Slavin, and its Middle East correspondent, Lara S. Korte, for a news segment on accusations of editorial interference at Stars and Stripes.

Earlier this month, the publisher, Max D. Lederer Jr., who had given Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte permission for the CBS interview, refused to fire them despite the urging of the Pentagon. After continued pressure, Mr. Lederer announced that he would retire by Sept. 30 and issued public statements on his strife with the Pentagon leadership. He was fired last Friday.

Ms. Korte and Mr. Slavin were also given termination notices last Friday, which cited insubordination and an unauthorized media appearance. In a statement at the time, Mr. Slavin said, “According to the notice, I am being fired for stating in a CBS interview that censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line.”

Mr. Lederer’s termination notice charged him with insubordination for refusing to deliver the notices of dismissal, according to the complaint.

Mr. Lederer, Ms. Korte and Mr. Slavin are now challenging their dismissals in court.

Their lawsuit says the Defense Department moved to fire Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte a day after Stars and Stripes published an article on the Abraham Lincoln, detailing how its sailors endured food and water shortages, disrupted mail service, long workdays, little time off and poor physical and mental health as a result of the carrier’s extended deployment.

For decades, federal regulations and Pentagon policy emphasized editorial integrity of Stars and Stripes, requiring “a free flow of news and information to its readership without news management or censorship.” Congress created the watchdog position in 1991, designing it to report directly to lawmakers and to ensure the publication’s independent reporting, acting after repeated attempts by military commanders who tried to censor the paper’s content in the 1980s.

During World War II, when General George Patton tried to dismiss a Stars and Stripes cartoonist for poking fun at the general’s order that soldiers be shaved clean even during combat, General Dwight D. Eisenhower dissuaded him.

“Stars and Stripes is the soldiers’ paper,” Eisenhower told Patton, “and we won’t interfere.”

In January, the Pentagon rescinded that 20-page regulation in its entirety. Its chief spokesman, Sean Parnell, said in a social media post that Stars and Stripes, which is primarily read by U.S. service members and their families, must “refocus its content away from woke distractions.” That same month, the Defense Department started asking applicants to Stars and Stripes to say how they would support Mr. Trump’s policies in their work.

In March, the Pentagon issued a memo banning the paper from running comics and reprinting articles from The Associated Press. The memo said Stars and Stripes’s news articles “must be consistent with good order and discipline of the military.” Critics say that language suppresses certain speech.

The journalists are calling now asking the judge to “declare unlawful” the March memo and the January deletion of regulations on the newspaper operations.

They also asked the judge to rule by Friday to temporarily block their firings while the case proceeds. The Pentagon gave the journalists only five days to respond to the termination notices, contrary to its own regulations that require a 30-day response period, according to the complaint.

item.title: Kansas Judge Dismisses Murder Charge Against Sheriff’s Deputy
item.description:
A Kansas judge dismissed a murder case on Thursday against a sheriff’s deputy who was accused last year of fatally kneeling on a handcuffed inmate, the county prosecutor’s office and the deputy’s lawyer said.

Prosecutors indicated that they would appeal the judge’s decision to drop all charges against the deputy, Richard Fatherley, who had been accused of second-degree murder in the July 2025 death of Charles Adair at the jail in Kansas City, Kan.

The death of Mr. Adair, who had been arrested based on misdemeanor warrants related to traffic tickets, prompted outcry last year in the Kansas City region and is the subject of an unresolved federal lawsuit.

Mr. Adair, who used a wheelchair and had several medical problems, was being wheeled back to his cell after having a dressing on his leg rewrapped when he got into a dispute with a deputy, according to an affidavit filed in court. Mr. Adair at that point threw himself out of his wheelchair, the filing said. He was then handcuffed, put back in the chair and wheeled to his cell, where deputies placed him on the bottom bunk, the affidavit said.

Mr. Adair, who remained handcuffed, was heard yelling “help,” the affidavit said. Deputy Fatherley then approached Mr. Adair and put his left knee on Mr. Adair’s lower back, while other Wyandotte County deputies held down other parts of his body, according to the affidavit.

Deputy Fatherley continued to hold Mr. Adair down until shortly after the handcuffs were removed, the affidavit said. A nurse soon entered the cell, where Mr. Adair was found to be unresponsive, the affidavit said. He was later pronounced dead, and an autopsy classified the death as a homicide.

The Kansas City Star reported on Thursday that Judge Aaron Roberts found that prosecutors had not met their burden for the case to proceed from a preliminary hearing to a trial. A written ruling from Judge Roberts, of the State District Court in Wyandotte County, was not immediately published on the court docket.

James L. Spies, a lawyer for Deputy Fatherley, said his client was “tremendously relieved” by the judge’s decision.

“My client never set out to harm him, never set out to do wrong by Mr. Adair,” Mr. Spies said.

The district attorney’s office in Wyandotte County said in an unsigned statement that it had already filed a notice of appeal.

“We respect the law, but disagree with the decision,” the statement said.

An attempt to reach lawyers for the Adair family was not immediately successful.

item.title: Progressives Condemn Pick of Pro-Israel Democrat Atop House Panel
item.description:
A backlash is underway within Democratic ranks after House leaders named a vocally pro-Israel Democrat to their top slot on a key panel that oversees Middle East policy, the latest reflection of bitter divisions in the party over support for the Jewish state.

Democrats on Tuesday chose Representative Jared Moskowitz of Florida to serve as the ranking member of the Foreign Affairs Committee’s Middle East and North Africa Subcommittee, elevating a lawmaker facing a tough re-election race who has called for “unwavering support” for Israel. Mr. Moskowitz has backed continued U.S. aid to Israel even as many Democrats have turned against it, and aggressively condemns critics of the Jewish state.

The selection put Mr. Moskowitz in line to lead the panel should Democrats win control of the House in November. Leaders also placed two other staunchly pro-Israel Democrats on the panel, Representatives Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida and Wesley Bell of Missouri, who like Mr. Moskowitz have been heavily backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

Progressives immediately condemned the moves, calling them tone-deaf and a sign that Democratic leaders have failed to grasp how voters in their own party have shifted on the issue of Israel and Gaza.

“Don’t put Israel hawks out of touch with our voters in charge of our Middle East policy,” Representative Ro Khanna, Democrat of California, warned party leaders on social media.

Some Democrats pushed back, noting that Mr. Moskowitz just last week trounced the progressive Democratic primary challenger in his South Florida district, who described himself as anti-Zionist.

But others asserted that the move was badly out of step with the party’s base.

In a series of irate posts, Benjamin J. Rhodes, a former top foreign policy adviser to President Barack Obama, wrote that Democrats were “showing zero regard for the vast majority of their own voters,” adding that their “disregard for war crimes and voter concerns could not be clearer.”

A New York Times/Siena national poll conducted in May found that 74 percent of Democratic voters opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel, and a Pew Research Center poll in April found that eight in 10 Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents had an unfavorable view of Israel.

The furor underscored the shift underway among Democrats over support for Israel — once seen as a prerequisite for anyone who wanted a future in politics, but now regarded by many in the party as a major liability. It also reinforced the looming challenge that Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat and minority leader, who is in line to be speaker should his party win the House, will face trying to govern a caucus in which Israel has become a major fault line.

Last month, when Mr. Jeffries called for a “major reset” between the United States and Israel, progressives took it as a positive sign that he was finally moving in their direction on a high-priority issue that has starkly divided the party.

But the selection of Mr. Moskowitz, who initially said he would oppose a resolution to rein in President Trump’s war powers in Iran before changing his mind, appeared to have alienated them anew.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations, a Muslim advocacy organization, said in a statement that the appointment of Mr. Moskowitz was “an insult to the American people and a desperate attempt to shield Israel from accountability.”

An overwhelming majority of Democrats “want to spend American taxpayer dollars here at home, not on bombing children overseas,” the organization said, adding that Congress should “reflect the will of the American people, not the wishes of AIPAC or Benjamin Netanyahu’s racist, genocidal government.”

A spokesman for Mr. Jeffries declined to comment.

If Mr. Moskowitz were to become the chairman of the subcommittee next year, he would decide hearing topics and choose witnesses, moves that help frame the issue and set the tone for the debate about Israel. Progressives said they feared that with someone like Mr. Moskowitz leading the panel, it would not address issues such as settler violence and humanitarian aid in Gaza.

While the appointment drew outrage from progressives, top House Democrats regarded it as a politically wise move given that Mr. Moskowitz faces a challenging re-election campaign in a district that has been redrawn to lean more conservative. They also noted that it represented no real ideological change from the way the panel is currently organized.

The current ranking Democrat on the Middle East panel, Representative Brad Sherman of California, is also staunchly pro-Israel. Mr. Sherman was willing to give up his position at the request of Mr. Moskowitz, who currently leads a different subcommittee but said the move would help him with pro-Israel Jews in his re-election campaign, according to two people familiar with the arrangement. Democrats who sit on the committee agreed to the change.

Some moderate Democrats said the backlash to Mr. Moskowitz’s appointment had been manufactured by the left.

“Are Democrats trying to tell other Democrats that supporters of the U.S.-Israeli relationship aren’t welcome in leadership positions — and who is next?” said Representative Josh Gottheimer, a centrist Democrat from New Jersey and a staunch supporter of Israel. “Is this a new litmus test for committee chairs? Moskowitz is beyond qualified.”

He called the progressive outrage “selective” and politically misguided, noting that it was coming as many in the party are encouraging pro-Israel Democrats to swallow their concerns about Abdul El-Sayed, the nominee for Senate in Michigan who is a vocal critic of Israel.

“This election should be about affordability and Trump’s corruption, and they want to make it about Jews and Israel,” Mr. Gottheimer said.

The decision cheered center-leaning Democrats and some donors, who said it indicated that Mr. Jeffries would not allow the party to be taken over by the demands of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Mr. Moskowitz, on social media, expressly thanked Mr. Jeffries for giving him “this important responsibility to help lead Democrats policy in the Middle East.”

item.title: White House Construction May Have Contributed to Close Call With Trump’s Helicopter
item.description:
Construction at the White House might have contributed to an incident this month in which President Trump’s helicopter came dangerously close to a commercial jet over Washington, according to a new report from the National Transportation Safety Board.

According to the report, work to build a new ballroom at the White House forced officials to move the helicopter’s takeoff location temporarily from the South Lawn to the Ellipse, the park south of the White House. But the new location might have been less optimal for communicating with air traffic controllers, leading to communication glitches, the report said.

Technicians “conducted a coverage analysis and determined that there was not adequate line-of-sight to ensure communications” between the Ellipse and the tower “while construction was ongoing at the White House,” the board’s report reads. There had been no known issues with the radio frequency before the incident.

The report chronicled how garbled communications caused the airport controller to miss multiple warnings from the helicopter crew that they were minutes from takeoff — a notification that would have signaled to the controller to temporarily ground planes while the helicopter passed through the area. Instead, the controller allowed an Envoy Air jet bound for Pensacola, Fla., to depart from an airport runway just as Marine One was about to take off, resulting in the plane and the helicopter passing each other less than a mile apart.

The board’s findings are preliminary, and its investigation of the incident is ongoing.

The White House grounds have been the site of extensive construction, as crews work 20 hours a day, seven days a week, to make progress on Mr. Trump’s plans to build a massive ballroom. The project has been hotly contested, but last week, the Supreme Court temporarily allowed Mr. Trump to forge ahead while it considered whether the 90,000-square-foot project could be completed.

Representatives for the White House did not address questions about the role that the White House ballroom construction might have played in the incident.

“Marine One flights are piloted by the finest aviators in the world, and the White House maintains the utmost confidence in these patriots and other security officials who are responsible for ensuring the president’s safety,” Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, said in a statement. “Although the president was at no point in harm’s way during the Aug. 4 momentary loss of separation, the White House continues to work with relevant military, F.A.A., and other security personnel to ensure the president’s continued safety.”

Under current procedures, controllers are expected to keep the congested skies around Ronald Reagan National Airport clear of traffic when the president’s helicopter is traversing the area.

In the wake of the Aug. 4 incident, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said that the president was never in danger because the flight paths of the two aircraft would not have converged. He blamed the incident on faulty telecom issues. Earlier this week, Bryan Bedford, who leads the Federal Aviation Administration, told reporters that his agency had made changes to communication procedures and had relocated an air traffic antenna to help fix the problems.

“The F.A.A. took immediate action following the Aug. 4 incident involving Marine One,” Hannah Walden, an F.A.A. spokeswoman, said in a statement, listing the changes that Mr. Bedford had referred to earlier in the week.

But those changes might not have fully addressed the problem. On Thursday, just hours after the N.T.S.B. released its preliminary report, air traffic controllers again appeared to have difficulty receiving transmissions from Marine One, just minutes before it was due to depart the Ellipse. They relied on other helicopters operating nearby to prepare for the president’s departure.

“Eagle 2, Marine One is trying to reach you at three minutes to lift,” one helicopter was heard radioing the control tower at Reagan National, according to transmissions captured on LiveATC.net, a site that compiles and posts recordings of air traffic audio collected by aviation enthusiasts.

“Oh, I couldn’t hear any of that,” the controller responded.

“Do me a favor: I can’t hear Marine One,” the controller said a couple of minutes later to another helicopter pilot. “If you hear Marine One, can you let me know?”

A little more than a minute later, the controller could be heard making contact with the Marine One crew, and the takeoff proceeded without incident, with controllers halting other traffic before takeoff. When asked about the incident, Ms. Walden said in a statement that the sequence had been smooth.

“The three-minute notification was communicated by alternate means, acknowledged by a controller, and positive contact was established with Marine One before takeoff,” she said.

But the events nonetheless harked back to last year’s tragic collision over National Airport, in which a passenger jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided in midair, killing 67. That accident focused national scrutiny on longstanding shortfalls in air traffic control staffing, and revealed that senior F.A.A. officials had ignored years of warnings that crisscrossing flight paths through the skies surrounding the airport posed critical safety risks.

In the months that followed, the F.A.A. took steps to reroute helicopter flight paths through the area, allowing only the most important government rotorcraft — such as Marine One — to traverse the airspace, and only when other flight traffic was grounded. The agency also ended the practice of visual separation, by which overtaxed controllers left helicopter pilots on their own to “see and avoid” oncoming airplane traffic, near busy airports like Ronald Reagan National Airport.

But critics, including most of the families of the victims of last year’s fatal crash, say the moves are not enough to avoid a repeat of a similar disaster.

The victims’ families have lobbied for new laws to force the F.A.A. to require that all aircraft be equipped with advanced technology that would allow pilots to track real-time location signals from other aircraft, arguing that would reduce their reliance on air traffic controllers to alert them to potential collision risks. An N.T.S.B. report into last year’s crash determined that if the airplane and helicopter had been equipped with such technology, the pilots would have had almost a minute’s forewarning that they were on a collision course, giving them ample time to avoid each other.

Efforts to enact such legislation, however, have been gridlocked for months as lawmakers in the House and Senate bicker over two competing approaches, which differ over what airplanes would be required to carry such technology and how strictly the military would be curtailed, statutorily, from turning off its location-broadcasting equipment when flying through restricted airspace.

item.title: Trump Administration Will Appeal Harvard Antisemitism Case
item.description:
The Justice Department moved Thursday to appeal a federal judge’s dismissal of a Trump administration lawsuit that accused Harvard University of illegally tolerating antisemitism.

The department filed a terse notice that did not detail the argument it will make to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. But it signaled the government was continuing its pressure campaign against the nation’s oldest university.

In its lawsuit against Harvard, filed in March, the Justice Department argued that the university had “turned a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis" and allowed years-ago protesters of the war in Gaza to defy Harvard rules “with impunity.”

A federal judge in Boston, Richard G. Stearns, ruled on Aug. 13 that the government was relying on accounts of antisemitism that were “too isolated and episodic” to support a finding that Harvard was violating civil rights law.

Judge Stearns concluded that the Trump administration, which had suggested it wanted to use a ruling in its favor to curb federal funding to Harvard, had not proven even “a plausible inference that any institutionalized noncompliance with Title VI persists at Harvard to this day.”

The law, the judge said, was intended to entice schools into protecting civil rights, not penalize them for previous failures.

The university did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

item.title: Man Flees Fire at His Home in Stolen Rescue Truck, Police Say
item.description:
A homeowner in rural New Hampshire found the most unusual time to take an early morning joyride, according to the authorities.

Even more unusual was his choice of vehicle: a rescue truck, which he stole from the emergency responders who were fighting a blaze that eventually gutted his home before sunrise on Tuesday morning, court documents show.

Nestor Roman II, 30, who lived in the home in Dalton, a town of about 900 residents on the Vermont state line, is facing felony charges of reckless conduct with a deadly weapon, stemming from his departure from the active fire scene at his home.

In this case, the weapon that officials said Mr. Roman used is a red 2009 Ford F-550 truck belonging to the Whitefield Fire Department. After Mr. Roman drove off, he nearly struck two firefighters and almost pinned a third firefighter between two large trucks, the Dalton Fire Department said in a statement online.

Mr. Roman also struck and damaged another Whitefield fire engine, which was “actively engaged” in fighting the fire at his home, officials said, adding that he drove over hoses and struck and damaged wooden fences at two other properties.

The damaged fire engine was able to continue operating, and the fire was extinguished. No firefighters were injured, officials said.

The cause of the fire is under investigation, officials said, and the two-bedroom, 1,200-square-foot home was destroyed.

A lawyer for Mr. Roman, Jay Duguay, did not respond to requests for comment on Thursday afternoon.

New Hampshire State Police troopers said they later received a report from a homeowner in Dalton that the stolen rescue vehicle had crashed on their property a few miles away. The caller also reported that Mr. Roman was trying to take items from their porch.

The troopers found Mr. Roman on the porch, they said, and he was arrested, after initially resisting them.

Both the rescue vehicle that Mr. Roman drove and the fire engine that he struck are out of service, the Whitefield fire chief, John Ross Jr., said in an email on Thursday. He could not say how much damage had been done, adding that he was meeting with an insurance adjuster on Friday.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Trump Plans to Mark 9/11 at the Pentagon, Not Ground Zero
item.description:
President Trump is not planning to attend a ceremony in Manhattan for the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center, in part because he wanted to deliver a speech and the annual event no longer allows them, according to four people with knowledge of the events.

Mr. Trump’s team had conducted advance visits at the site and had initially signaled to officials in New York and in Washington that the president intended to visit the memorial space known as ground zero, two of the people with knowledge of the events said.

The president’s interest in speaking on Sept. 11 was conveyed to memorial planners in recent weeks, three of the people with knowledge of the events said. But since 2012, politicians have been barred from speaking at the site. The National September 11 Memorial and Museum, which oversees the site, has worked rigorously to keep the venue nonpartisan and focused on the solemnity of the day.

Mr. Trump, a native New Yorker who talked often about the Sept. 11 attacks during his 2016 presidential campaign, is now expected to commemorate them at the Pentagon, two of the people with knowledge of the events said. The Pentagon also came under attack on Sept. 11, 2001.

Vice President JD Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.

The president will go to the Pentagon after he attends a midterm political convention in Texas. Officials have discussed some kind of tribute to the terrorist attack victims during that convention, which takes place Sept. 9 and 10.

There are other considerations that led to Mr. Trump honoring the day in Washington, including that he will depart the next day for his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where the Irish Open tournament will take place. Leaving from John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City, or from Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, would snarl air and motor traffic to a much greater extent than with Mr. Trump leaving from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

Mr. Trump last attended the ceremony at ground zero in 2024, when he stood alongside Mr. Vance, former Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg, President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Vice President Kamala Harris.

None of the officials made formal remarks. Mr. Trump visited a fire station in New York City after the event.

This year’s anniversary marks a quarter-century since the worst attack on the United States after the assault on Pearl Harbor. Anna Kelly, a spokeswoman for the White House, did not address the president’s plans in a response to an email seeking comment.

“On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the president will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans,” she said.

At the Pentagon, Mr. Trump will be allowed to speak, as he did last year, when he attended the remembrances there. His speech that day came less than 24 hours after the conservative activist Charlie Kirk, whose efforts to draw college-aged voters into the MAGA movement were seen as significant to Mr. Trump’s 2024 victory, was shot and killed while speaking on a campus in Utah.

The ceremony had been intended to be held in a different spot that day, but was moved to a new one amid security concerns about the president after Mr. Kirk was assassinated.

“We recall the light of America’s best and bravest and the love that they showed in their final moments,” Mr. Trump said at the time. “In their memory, we make a solemn pledge and a noble promise. We will honor always our great heroes, and you are our heroes.”

The president has faced two assassination attempts and other murder-for-hire plots by alleged Iranian proxies. He has faced an uptick in threats since he began a war against Iran on Feb. 28.

This year’s event in Manhattan is expected to include former Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani; former President Bill Clinton and his wife, Hillary Clinton; former President George W. Bush and his wife, Laura; and President Barack Obama, among others, according to several people who have been close to the planning.

In the first decade after Sept. 11, elected officials would read poems and historic American documents, like the Gettysburg Address, at the ceremony. But since 2012, the memorial has barred any speeches by politicians. Instead, politicians stand alongside their peers from opposing parties as families step onto a stage to read the names of the dead over the course of hours.

Mr. Trump’s advisers have discussed possibly taking federal control of the National September 11 Memorial and Museum, including as recently as last year. Families of the Sept. 11 victims have in recent years criticized the site over its leadership and finances.

Mr. Trump, who was in New York on the day of the attacks, spoke to a New Jersey television station in the aftermath, saying that a building he owned had gained in stature because the twin towers had fallen. That building, 40 Wall Street, “actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually — before the World Trade Center — was the tallest.”

He went on, “And then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest. And now it’s the tallest.” (The statement was not correct; 70 Pine Street, nearby, was taller than Mr. Trump’s building.)

item.title: Climber Stranded for Hours on 6-Inch Rock Ledge Before Rescue
item.description:
A man climbing a mountain in the Sierra Nevada in California on Saturday was stranded for roughly eight hours, his body shaking as he balanced on a six-inch ledge at an elevation of 10,600 feet, before a dramatic rescue.

According to rescuers, the man and a friend had been climbing Mendenhall Couloir, a gully carved into Laurel Mountain in the Inyo National Forest. It is, at times, a vertical face.

The pair were not using ropes, which are not considered necessary for experienced climbers here, to ascend the 11,818-foot mountain, said Mitch Quiring, the public information officer for the Mono County search and rescue team, which conducted the operation. The man had followed a band of red rock, an established route, but stepped away from the route and became stuck on a ledge, he said.

“Having a couple of wrong moves,” Mr. Quiring said, “leads you to the brink of quite literally a life-altering decision.”

The route for Mendenhall Couloir can be hard to find at times, said Clay Tyson, the owner of Ground Up Climbing Guides, a local climbing service. “You can think you’re in the right zone,” Mr. Tyson said, “but it’s tricky.”

In similar situations, officials might have opted for a helicopter rescue, but high winds on Saturday made that too dangerous, Mr. Quiring said.

Saturday was an unusually windy day for the area, said Emily Wilson, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s office in Hanford, Calif. Wind gusts reached up to 50 miles an hour around a similar elevation on Mammoth Mountain, about an hour from where the climber was clinging to the tiny ledge, she said.

The climber, whose name has not been released, called 911 around 1:20 p.m., according to the Mono County search and rescue team, a nonprofit group composed of volunteers. Mr. Quiring and a rescue partner were dropped off by a helicopter on Laurel Mountain, ascended about 1,000 feet and crested the peak, which looks out over Convict Lake.

For more than two hours, they looked for the climber, to no avail, even with the help of a helicopter pilot. GPS coordinates provided by the climber were not precise, Mr. Quiring said.

As the rescuers searched, their whistles and calls bounced off the rock. The wind often carried away their shouts, he said. “It’s like being in a hallway of mirrors,” he said. “It’s like, ‘Where exactly is that coming from?’”

But eventually, the climber’s voice pierced the wind, and the rescuers were able to spot his white and orange helmet against the gray rock, Mr. Quiring said. Relief washed over the climber.

But he was still in apparent distress, Mr. Quiring said, hopping from one foot to another, apparently to stave off a cramp.

The sun was beginning to set behind Laurel Mountain, and the dark and cold of nightfall brought new urgency. “He had been holding on and fighting and fighting,” Mr. Quiring said. “But it was our belief, at the time, that he would run out of that sustainability to remain safely on that ledge if we had left him overnight.”

In all, four rescuers devised a plan via radio and clicked on their headlamps in the pitch dark. With a meticulous system of bolts and ropes, they reached the climber. His friend, who had gotten ahead of him, reached the summit and was in touch with the crew during the rescue.

All together, the rescuers and the rescued climbed up the mountain, without ropes, and reached the zenith. It was 12:45 a.m., and the temperature had dropped below 50 degrees. Eventually, a car drove them off Laurel Mountain.

The man had been stuck for eight to nine hours.

“He did not give up, and that is really one of the biggest takeaways from this,” Mr. Quiring said. “This could have been a very different story if he didn’t push through the adversity.”

item.title: ‘I Need to Go to the Hospital,’ Delta Pilot Tells Air Traffic Control
item.description:
The altitude read 39,000 feet. The speed was hovering around 600 miles per hour. And the compass pointed due east.

But just after crossing over Lake Michigan on Tuesday, a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to Boston declared an emergency, leaving its course hundreds of miles short of its destination. Flight 437 had to land.

The captain of the Boeing 757 told air traffic controllers that someone was experiencing a medical episode, not one of the 147 passengers, but himself, the rare occurrence playing out over radio transmissions from the cockpit.

The transcontinental flight diverted safely to Detroit under the control of the first officer before another crew completed it, according to Delta. The trip normally takes between five and five-and-a-half hours.

On its final descent into Detroit Metro Airport, a Delta hub, the pilot explained his predicament to the tower.

“This is the captain,” the pilot said, “I’m the one that’s ill. I’m going to taxi the jet to the gate, and then I need to go to the hospital.”

The pilot did not specify what kind of medical issue he was dealing with during the exchange with the air traffic controller, who said the Delta flight was clear to use taxiway Yankee 2 so that it could reach the terminal faster.

But after the plane landed on Runway 22 Left, some confusion emerged about the gate that had been assigned to the flight.

“It says the gate is Alpha 13, but it doesn’t look like it exists,” the pilot told the controller, who responded that A-13 was not large enough to accommodate a Boeing 757 in the first place.

The flight was directed to gate A-10.

In a statement, Delta Air Lines apologized for the disruption and said the flight had landed “uneventfully.”

The airline confirmed that the captain had handled communication with air traffic controllers while the first officer landed the plane, which it described as standard operating procedure.

Delta did not answer questions about the pilot’s condition or his symptoms.

Kit Darby, a retired United Airlines captain and a former instructor pilot for Delta and Boeing, said in an interview on Thursday that instances of commercial airline pilots experiencing a medical episode and declaring an emergency were rare.

Airlines have safeguards in place when that happens, he said: the other pilot and the autopilot.

“The airplane can be flown, landed and taxied with one pilot,” said Mr. Darby, an aviation consultant who has flown several aircraft models, including the Boeing 757 and the Boeing 767. “It’s redundant.”

He said that pilots are trained to check for signs that another pilot might be in distress, such as if a plane starts to deviate from the course it has been cleared to fly by air traffic controllers.

“The guy sounds perfectly normal,” Mr. Darby said of the pilot’s exchange with the airport tower.

On the Boeing 757, the controls for steering the plane while it is on the ground are positioned next to the left cockpit seat, which would require the pilots to switch seats if one could not perform his or her duties, Mr. Darby said. It was not clear if the captain and first officer of the Delta flight had switched seats.

Before Flight 437 departed Los Angeles International Airport, both the pilot and the first officer would have been required to sign a release attesting that they were fit for duty that would have been submitted to an airline station agent at the gate.

“It states that they are physically and mentally fit to fly the flight and they’ve done the things necessary to make the flight safe,” Mr. Darby said.

item.title: Lake Ontario Didn’t Ask for This
item.description:
Americans hadn’t seen President Trump in a few days, not since he diverted from an education policy event on Monday to give reporters a tour of the new helipad he is building on the South Lawn of the White House.

A curious citizen may wonder: What has Mr. Trump been up to in the days since we last saw our wartime president? What are his priorities?

We all got an answer on Thursday, when Mr. Trump decided to take a private event, previously billed as a “Signing Time” session on his daily schedule, and make it public. He beckoned reporters into the Oval Office, where he sat next to a large poster of the Great Lakes, which were displayed alongside the words “Making The Great Lakes Even Greater.”

This is not really possible, as the Great Lakes are perfect as they are. But Mr. Trump decided to bump renaming Lake Ontario to the top of his priority list anyway. With a flourish of his executive-order Sharpie, Mr. Trump rechristened the body of water Lake America, sticking it to the Canadians as trade negotiations continued to devolve.

This was only Mr. Trump’s latest maximally patriotic (and some may say, diplomatically petty) branding exercise meant to slight an old ally. On the first day of his second term, Mr. Trump pulled out that Sharpie and — Presto! — turned the Gulf of Mexico into the Gulf of America, as part of a broader effort to “honor American greatness.” On Thursday, Mr. Trump also mused that he would rename an ocean and complete the set.

As one of the five Great Lakes of North America, Lake Ontario didn’t ask for this. The lake existed peacefully long before humans arrived and started divvying up their shares. Now, there is a dividing line between the United States and Canada, drawn right through the pancreas-shaped body of water. Mr. Trump’s executive order asserts that the deepest waters of the lake are located in the United States, along with most of the lake’s volume.

Inside the Oval Office, a reporter asked Mr. Trump a question relevant to his priorities: Why target allies over adversaries?

“Well, they haven’t treated us well,” Mr. Trump said. “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly; they’re nasty people. They charge our farmers 400 percent tariffs. They’ve been doing it for a long time. And I had them figured out in my first term, and I did some pretty strong things and had it getting pretty good. And then the election was rigged and now I’m coming back and doing it the way it — and finishing the job.”

(Mr. Trump has repeatedly claimed that the Canadians bring exorbitant tariffs against American farmers, and those past assertions, just like this one, were misleading.)

Mr. Trump’s rebranding-focused executive orders can direct federal agencies to adopt the new names, but other countries do not have to acknowledge the change, and the Canadians definitely do not seem interested in doing so.

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big”. The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada wrote on X — in English, and in French — in a rebuttal to Mr. Trump’s decision. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, has grown frustrated with souring trade talks and escalating lake threats in recent days, and has said the president could kiss a certain body part — the French call it a derrière. On Thursday, though, Mr. Ford issued a succinct response: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”

And so goes another Thursday in the doldrums of Mr. Trump’s August, when he has poked his head up long enough to cause a diplomatic disturbance before retreating out of the public eye to turn to other pressing matters. (Some supporters suggested that this was all a highly strategic way to whip the news media up: “Trump Controls the News Cycle Volume 87187585124782,” Tricia McLaughlin, a former Department of Homeland Security spokeswoman, wrote on X in support of Mr. Trump’s work today.)

On his Air Force One flight to a (private) Republican National Committee event in Houston, Mr. Trump kept the public updated on staffing — Ben Moss is the new White House staff secretary — and his thoughts on presidential performance, posting a graphic of past presidents next to rankings ranging from “THE GREATEST” (take a wild guess) to “FAILURES” (now take another one). He posted an image declaring that the war in Iran was “MISSION ACCOMPLISHED” — not quite true — and he congratulated Nvidia on a record sales year.

He eventually circled back to the matter of renaming the lake, posting a letter from Dr. Ned Mamula, the director of the U.S. Geological Survey, who told him that his wish had been granted.

“The change will begin occurring in printed documents over the next several days,” Dr. Mamula wrote.

Mr. Trump’s job approval rating has reached record lows. The war he began against Iran turns six months old on Friday, which is about five months longer than he had originally promised. And old allies — the Canadians, of all people — are growing comfortable showing greater degrees of defiance in the face of Mr. Trump’s threat.

But at least this mission, this matter of renaming a lake, was accomplished.

item.title: Los Angeles Mayor, Stung in Debate, Eases Street Vending Crackdown
item.description:
Mayor Karen Bass has eased a crackdown on Los Angeles street vendors after she compared them with homeless encampments last week, setting off fierce criticism and creating a flashpoint in her re-election campaign.

During a heated debate with Nithya Raman, a progressive Democrat whom Ms. Bass will face in November’s election, the mayor said that she did not believe that vendors should be allowed to sell food in front of restaurants.

“I do not think that you should have a food vendor in front of a restaurant. Period,” Ms. Bass said, suggesting that the vendors should be restricted to certain locations, and, eventually, move into brick-and-mortar facilities.

“You can move that person so that person can have a living, make money, but not right in front of a restaurant that discourages patrons from going in,” she said. “Just like you shouldn’t have encampments in front of restaurants, or in front of schools.”

The comments angered some vendors and others who criticized Ms. Bass for conflating them with homeless people. They said the comment showed that the mayor was out of touch with what many consider to be one of the most beloved parts of Los Angeles’s food culture.

“These are individuals who are moms, who are our uncles, who work legitimately, who wake up really early,” said Sergio Jimenez, who has organized with street vendors across Los Angeles for close to a decade.

“They’re not addicts. They’re not taking funds from the government,” he said, adding that many had fought for years to legalize parts of their industry. “It was like a slap in the face,” he said.

Across the sprawling city, vendors serve tamales from coolers, assemble flame-roasted meat on hot tortillas and grill bacon-wrapped sausages until crispy. They pop up on corners, in parking lots and outside grocery stores. Some have folding tables for patrons. Their food is far cheaper than what many restaurants offer. Yet many are just as well known and beloved — with lines often stretching down the road.

Historically, street vending has also been an easily accessible profession for new immigrants who may not have the resources to open a brick-and-mortar shop, and they offer a familiar taste of home to Angelenos far from their home countries.

Under state law, sidewalk vending is decriminalized, though vendors must follow local regulations and obtain permits. But advocates say that the police have sometimes used an anti-camping ordinance to issue citations to vendors at MacArthur Park, a hub in one of Los Angeles’s most immigrant-heavy neighborhoods. Mr. Jimenez said he had worked with about a dozen vendors who he believed had been wrongly cited.

In a statement on Thursday, Ms. Bass’s office said she “stands firmly with street vendors” and had directed the Los Angeles Police Department to stop issuing them criminal citations, and to dismiss those issued in error, “ensuring they are not left with criminal records for working to provide for their families.”

Paige Sterling, a spokeswoman for Ms. Bass, said that the police had informed Ms. Bass’s office that criminal citations had been issued in error around MacArthur Park. The mayor’s office has asked the police to confirm that the issue was not more widespread, the spokeswoman said.

“Street vending is a quintessential part of L.A.’s world-class food scene and a livelihood for thousands of hard-working Angelenos,” her office said, noting that it had spent nearly $500,000 this fiscal year on a joint program with Los Angeles County that helps vendors establish or grow their businesses.

The Los Angeles Police Department did not immediately respond to a request seeking more information on Thursday.

The dispute has further highlighted the divide between Ms. Bass, 72, a nationally known Democrat who has struggled to rebound since the Los Angeles wildfires, and Ms. Raman, a City Council member and former Bass ally who has drawn comparisons to New York’s democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

In recent months, the two candidates have clashed over policing, housing and homelessness — all evidence of an ideological and generational divide between the center-left Democratic establishment that has shaped the city for years, and young progressives. Ms. Raman, 44, has described the vendors as among the most vibrant and visible parts of the city’s economy.

In 2024, Ms. Raman backed a measure reducing the city’s vending permit fee to $27.51 from $541. She has criticized state laws and a confusing process that stops many stands from getting the health permits they need to operate legally.

Speaking at a taco stand on Wednesday, Ms. Raman said Ms. Bass “took a shot at street vendors” but that she planned to work with them to regulate and legalize operations.

Mr. Jimenez said that while there was a long way to go toward improving conditions, the news that the police would stop issuing criminal citations to vendors was “a positive step.”

item.title: Judge Once Again Bars Postal Service From Restricting Mail-In Vote
item.description:
A federal judge on Thursday once again temporarily prohibited the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan to restrict mail-in voting, put in place after a directive from President Trump.

Federal District Judge Indira Talwani had cleared the way for the Postal Service to move forward just the day before, but on Thursday, she issued a new order concluding that the agency’s plan, released late on Friday, appeared to overstep its legal mandate and could spark chaos by changing rules fewer than 70 days before an election.

She wrote that a group of Democratic-led states that had sued “face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible as to the 2026 midterm elections, now little more than two months away.”

“Most plaintiff states have already ordered their mail ballots, and some are required by state law to send them to eligible voters as early as next week,” she added.

She wrote that while the Supreme Court had “admonished” her on Monday that the Postal Service had not finalized any changes when the groups sued initially, making court action premature, the stakes had changed since then because of the step the agency took Friday to formalize its plan.

Her ruling marked the third court decision on the issue in less than a week, a whipsaw of action that threatened to confuse voters. But each delay has reduced the administration’s chances of clearing the legal hurdles to execute its logistically complicated mail-in ballot plan before the November election. She blocked the rule from taking effect for 14 days, and she had previously scheduled a hearing to discuss the legality of the rule on Sept. 3.

In her order, Judge Talwani explained that the prospect of the new rule suddenly taking effect carried “significant risk of their members’ disenfranchisement” for voting rights organizations, which had also sued, along with the states.

She ticked through a list of requirements that state election officials would be required to meet to ensure delivery of ballots, including receiving the agency’s approval for new envelope designs and submitting voters’ information into an online portal run by the Postal Service.

“Where a state or local election official does not obtain envelope and return envelope design approval, or does not upload voter information, or does not include unique intelligent mail bar codes on ballot envelopes, the U.S.P.S. will not mail ballots to voters,” she concluded.

In March, President Trump issued an executive order that required the Department of Homeland Security to create and circulate state-by-state citizenship lists to state officials. It further urged states to provide the U.S. Postal Service with their own lists of voters eligible to cast ballots by mail.

Multiple lawsuits were filed challenging the order, arguing that Congress and the states set rules for elections, not the executive branch. The challengers also argued that no federal law gives the Postal Service the power to make those kinds of election-related rules.

On Monday, the Supreme Court ruled that one suit, brought by a group of Democratic-led states, was premature because the administration had not started implementing its plans.

But late Friday, just before the court ruled, the Postal Service formally published a new plan to comply with the executive order. Under that plan, the service would not deliver mail ballots in states that do not share voter data with the agency and would only deliver ballots that meet certain criteria.

Lawyers for the Trump administration and the groups challenging the rule continue to clash over a straightforward issue: Whether or not the Postal Service’s plan would mean the agency would be taking on a new role verifying voters and potentially rejecting ballots in the midterm election in November.

In a filing on Thursday, the Postal Service denied that its proposal left room for the service to second-guess states on which voters were eligible to cast a ballot.

“U.S.P.S. will not scrutinize those decisions or alter that information in any way — instead leaving it entirely up to the states to accurately and lawfully identify its residents who are eligible to vote by mail,” the filing said. “The Postal Service will not determine voter eligibility, ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures.”

Instead, it described the changes as minor logistical improvements and streamlining, such as requiring voters to submit their addresses ahead of time to improve processing. It said the changes were designed “as a matter of the Postal Service’s own judgment.” Lawyers for the service argued it is authorized to adopt mail rules under statutes adopted by Congress.

A spokesman for the Postal Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The challengers argue that the Postal Service rule is an unconstitutional violation of the separation of powers, allowing the executive branch to intrude into elections. They say that no federal law permits such action by the agency, and they assert that the Trump administration’s actions are likely to sow confusion among voters and to lead to disenfranchisement.

The agency has said that it would not try to impose the new requirements for the 2026 elections, unless explicitly allowed to by the courts.

A series of lawsuits in Massachusetts and the District of Columbia by different groups have challenged Mr. Trump’s effort to discredit and erect obstacles to mail-in voting. The lawsuits have challenged both Mr. Trump’s executive order and the Postal Service rule, focusing on their implementation this year and beyond.

Adam Sella contributed reporting.
